overview: Late medieval Bosnia linked mountain settlements, mining districts and trading routes to the Adriatic. Kings shared power with influential noble families. Surviving coins, textiles and carved tombstones reveal skilled work and social differences; the atlas interval continues beyond the royal kingdom’s collapse in 1463.

periods.title: A kingdom of towns and regional lords
periods.summary: Mining and commerce supported royal and noble households, artisans and growing settlements.

periods.title: Conquest and contested territories
periods.summary: Ottoman conquest ended the royal kingdom in 1463; Hungarian counterattacks left some districts contested.

sections.title: Work that connected mountains and ports

items.text: Srebrenica’s silver deposits made it an important mining and trading centre. Extraction required miners, processing skills and supplies. The value of exported metal helped sustain towns as well as the households of rulers.

Ragusan merchants established communities in places including Fojnica, Visoko and Foča. Local merchants also participated. Business involved credit, workshops and markets, rather than only dramatic journeys by wealthy visitors.

Silver travelled through Ragusa and onward to Venice, while salt and cloth were important imports. Vlach carriers helped move goods. Every distant purchase depended on the less glamorous work of loading and transporting it.

At Boljuni, inscriptions name makers such as Grubač and scribes such as Semorad. Carving the stone and composing its message could involve different specialists. These names let some craftspeople step out from behind their finished work.

Excavators at Kopošići in 2015 uncovered an oak coffin and unusually well-preserved brocade in a grave dated to the fifteenth century. The cloth originally had a purple background with lions or griffins, worked in gilded-silver threads.

The museum identifies the burial as Mirko Radojević’s using written evidence and a reported paternal relationship to the neighbouring burial of Batić Mirković. The name is an evidence-based attribution; DNA alone does not provide a historical person’s name.

The brocade was probably imported and records an elite family’s access to expensive material. Its survival is extraordinary, but this ceremonial burial garment cannot tell us what most villagers wore while farming or cooking.

Stećci are large medieval grave markers, often carved from limestone. Slabs, chests and other forms could carry images or writing. Their varied shapes show that commissioning remembrance involved choices about expense, skill and appearance.

These tombstones were used by Catholic, Orthodox and Church of Bosnia communities. They are not the exclusive signature of one religious group. Most were made in the 1300s and 1400s, within a longer regional tradition.

Ključ’s fortifications used steep terrain together with built defences. Different sections spread across the ridge. The setting helps explain why a stronghold’s effectiveness depended on landscape as well as the thickness of its walls.

A groš of Tvrtko II in the History Museum’s catalogue measures about 21 millimetres and weighs about two grams. Its shield carries a crowned T, with helmet and elaborate crest above: a compact royal announcement in metal.

DnS TuARTCO - REX BOSnE means “Lord Tvrtko, king of Bosnia.” This Latin legend appears on the catalogued fifteenth-century groš of Tvrtko II. The lettering is preserved as transcribed by the museum; a coin title does not imply universal literacy.

ending.text: Ottoman forces captured King Stjepan Tomašević in 1463, and Sultan Mehmed II ordered his execution. The royal kingdom ended, while Hungarian counterattacks and later campaigns produced changing frontiers. Towns, families and working communities continued under different rulers; 1492 is this map segment’s endpoint, not Bosnia’s extinction.
